Guided Inquiry

Look and listen (with your eyes)

Two pure tones are playing together: f₁ = 440 Hz and f₂ = 444 Hz. The top two traces are the individual tones; the bottom is their sum. Watch the sum swell and fade — that swelling is the beat.

The green curve tracing the outline of the sum is the beat envelope. Each bulge is one throb. The trace is drawn 60× slower than real so single cycles stay visible; the time axis underneath is in real seconds.

Predict: how many throbs in 10 seconds?

With f₁ = 440 Hz and f₂ = 444 Hz, how many loudness swells will you count in ten seconds?

Predict: bring f₂ toward f₁ — what happens to the throbs?

You are about to slide f₂ down from 444 Hz toward 440 Hz. What do the throbs do?

Now slide f₂ in toward f₁

Drag the f₂ slider in the sidebar downward. The bulges of the envelope grow wider; the meter's throb slows. Take f₂ all the way to 440 Hz — the beating stops. That is how a piano tuner tunes a string: eliminate the beats.

Watch the readouts: the beat frequency falls to zero and the beat period runs away to ∞, while the pitch — the average ½(f₁ + f₂) — barely moves at all.

Predict: does it matter how high the notes are?

Take a pair that beats 4 times a second: 440 Hz and 444 Hz. Now try 256 Hz and 260 Hz — a much lower pitch, same 4 Hz difference. What is the beat rate of the second pair?

The rule, made unmissable

The throb rate is the difference of the two frequencies and nothing else. Bring the frequencies together and the beating slows until it stops entirely at unison. Move both up together — the pitch rises, but the throbs are unchanged.

This is exactly how a piano tuner works: adjust the string until the beats vanish, and it is in tune.

Sum of two tones

Two sines of nearly equal frequency add to a fast tone modulated by a slow envelope.

Beat frequency

The throb rate is the difference of the two frequencies — because loudness peaks at both bulges of the modulating cosine.

Heard pitch (average)

The ear reads the pitch as the average of the two frequencies — completely separate from the throb rate.

Beat period

At unison, T_beat → ∞: there is no repetition, and no beating.

The Physics

Beats — When Two Notes Argue Slowly · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two pure tones of nearly the same frequency play together. The sim draws each tone, then their sum. The sum swells and fades, and that throbbing in loudness is called a beat.

What you'll learn

  • Why two nearby tones make a throbbing sound instead of a steady one.
  • How the throbbing is related to the two frequencies f₁ and f₂.
  • How the pitch you hear is related to them.
  • How a piano tuner uses the throbbing.
Two sources, one listener. The ear receives the sum of the two sound waves.

What's on screen

  • Tone 1 alone (top row): a steady wave at frequency f₁.
  • Tone 2 alone (middle row): a steady wave at frequency f₂.
  • Sum (bottom row): the two added together.
  • Envelope: the green outline that follows the peaks of the sum.
See itOpen the sim at its starting values. Watch for: two steady traces on top, and a sum below them whose height swells and fades inside the green envelope.

03

Two nearby tones drift in and out of step

Sound waves add: at each instant the sum is the first wave plus the second. When two tones have different frequencies, their crests do not stay lined up. At some moments the crests of both waves coincide, and the sum reaches its largest height. A little later a crest of one meets a trough of the other, and they cancel.

Because the two frequencies are almost equal, this change is slow. Over many cycles the sum keeps a tone of about the same pitch, while its height grows and shrinks. The green envelope traces that growing and shrinking. Each swell is one beat, heard as one throb in loudness.

With equal amplitudes the sum reaches twice the height of one tone, and falls to zero at its quietest moments.

See itKeep the starting values and let the traces run. Watch for: the bottom trace reaching +2 and −2 at the bulges, and shrinking to a point between them.
04

The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies

After one second, tone 1 has completed f₁ cycles and tone 2 has completed f₂ cycles. Tone 1 has gained |f₁ − f₂| cycles on tone 2. Each extra cycle takes the two waves from lined up, through opposed, and back to lined up: one swell. So:

fbeat = |f₁ − f₂|     Tbeat = 1 / |f₁ − f₂|
Throbs per second, and seconds per throb.

Algebra gives the same result: sin(2πf₁t) + sin(2πf₂t) = 2 cos(2π·½(f₁ − f₂)t) · sin(2π·½(f₁ + f₂)t). The cosine factor is the slow envelope. Its size |cos| peaks twice per cycle of the cosine, so the swells come at |f₁ − f₂|, not at half of it.

For 440 Hz and 444 Hz, fbeat = 4 Hz and Tbeat = 0.250 s. In ten seconds that is 40 throbs.

See itKeep f₁ = 440 Hz and f₂ = 444 Hz. Watch for: 4.00 Hz and 0.250 s in the readouts, with the envelope bulges 0.25 s apart on the time axis.
05

Bringing the tones together slows the beats until they stop

Because fbeat = |f₁ − f₂|, a smaller gap between the tones gives fewer throbs per second, and each one lasts longer. The envelope bulges stretch out.

  • f₂ = 442 Hz: fbeat = 2 Hz, Tbeat = 0.500 s.
  • f₂ = 441 Hz: fbeat = 1 Hz, Tbeat = 1.000 s.
  • f₂ = 440 Hz: fbeat = 0, so Tbeat is infinite. The two waves stay in step forever and the sum has a constant height.

The absolute value means it does not matter which tone is higher. The beats at f₂ = 436 Hz are the same as at 444 Hz.

See itSet f₂ = 440 Hz, equal to f₁. Watch for: 0.00 Hz and ∞ — no beats in the readouts, and a flat envelope with the label unison.
06

The pitch is the average, and beats ignore it

The fast factor in the product is sin(2π·½(f₁ + f₂)t). The ear hears this as one tone at the average frequency, fpitch = ½(f₁ + f₂). The sim shows it as "Pitch you hear".

The two quantities answer different questions. The pitch says how high the note sounds. The beat frequency says how fast it throbs. Only the gap |f₁ − f₂| enters the beat rate, so a pair far down the keyboard throbs exactly as fast as a pair far up it, if their gaps match.

  • 440 Hz and 444 Hz: pitch 442.0 Hz, fbeat = 4 Hz.
  • 256 Hz and 260 Hz: pitch 258.0 Hz, fbeat = 4 Hz.
See itSet f₁ = 256 Hz and f₂ = 260 Hz. Watch for: the beat frequency still at 4.00 Hz, with the pitch at 258.0 Hz.
07

Where it matters

  • Tuning. A piano tuner plays a string against a reference and adjusts it until the throbbing slows and stops. At unison the string matches the reference.
  • Measuring an unknown frequency. If a tuning fork of known f₁ beats at 3 Hz with an unknown source, f₂ is f₁ + 3 or f₁ − 3. Nudging the source slightly and seeing whether the beats speed up or slow down settles which.
  • Limits of hearing. Throbbing is heard clearly for gaps up to about ten hertz. A much larger gap sounds rough, and a larger one still sounds like two separate tones. The sim lets the gap grow to 300 Hz, where the pattern is still plotted but a real ear would not hear it as a throb.
  • Waves in general. The same arithmetic describes any two nearby frequencies, such as two radio signals or two light sources.
08

Summary

In one line. Two nearby tones add to a tone whose loudness swells and fades, and each swell is one beat.

Key points

  • fbeat = |f₁ − f₂| and Tbeat = 1/|f₁ − f₂|.
  • The pitch heard is ½(f₁ + f₂), separate from the beat rate.
  • At f₁ = f₂ the beating stops.

Common mix-ups

  • "Higher notes beat faster." Only the gap matters. 256 and 260 Hz beat as fast as 440 and 444 Hz.
  • "The beat is the average of the frequencies." The average is the pitch. The beat is the difference.
  • "Beats tell you which tone is higher." |f₁ − f₂| is the same either way.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the f₂ values that give a beat of 5 Hz when f₁ = 400 Hz.
  • Read the beat period straight off the time axis and compare it with the readout.
